title: Global military spending rose while US spending fell and European capacity accelerated
source_unit: SIPRI military-expenditure estimate by country, region, and alliance grouping
geography: Global, national, regional, and NATO groupings

world_spending.unit: US dollars billions at current prices

real_change.unit: percent change from 2024 in constant 2024 US dollars

decade_change.unit: percent change from 2016 to 2025 in real terms

observations.method: SIPRI estimates national and regional military expenditure from open sources, presents calendar-year figures in current and constant US dollars, and calculates GDP, government-expenditure, and per-capita shares using its Military Expenditure Database.
observations.uncertainty: Some country figures are estimated; financial-year and calendar-year conventions differ; open-source availability and national reporting quality vary. Global aggregates do not measure operational capability, readiness, procurement delivery, or welfare trade-offs.
observations.subgroup: World aggregate and regional/national military-spending units.
observations.counterinterpretation: A slower global growth rate can coexist with historically high spending; monetary totals do not show effectiveness, strategic intent, or how spending affects households and social programs.

us_to_china_ratio.unit: ratio of US to Chinese military spending in 2025

observations.method: SIPRI country estimates and rankings using current-price US-dollar totals and constant-dollar real-change calculations.
observations.uncertainty: China's figure is estimated; exchange rates, purchasing-power differences, classified spending, and assistance accounting affect comparisons. Spending is an input to capacity, not a direct measure of military output.
observations.subgroup: United States, China, Russia, Germany, and India; top-five aggregate.
observations.counterinterpretation: A falling US annual total can reflect a fall in supplemental overseas assistance rather than broad reductions in all US capabilities or procurement priorities.

nato_members_at_least_two_percent_gdp.unit: NATO members meeting at least 2.0% of GDP under SIPRI methodology

observations.method: SIPRI regional and alliance aggregation from national military-expenditure estimates.
observations.uncertainty: Alliance totals combine countries with different accounting, fiscal years, and estimates; the 2.0% threshold is a SIPRI calculation and does not measure readiness, burden-sharing quality, or political durability.
observations.subgroup: Europe, Asia and Oceania, NATO, and European NATO members.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher allied spending may improve material options without producing interoperable capability, timely procurement, or stable public support; lower US spending may reflect aid-accounting changes.

related_sources.claim: Official SIPRI metadata and replacement-vintage notice.
SIPRI Military Expenditure Database covering 1949–2025 and methodology.
Prior 2024 vintage retained for comparison; updated by the 2025 release.

boundary: This record measures SIPRI monetary estimates and shares of military expenditure through 2025. It does not establish operational capability, procurement realization, alliance behavior, state intent, household incidence, social-spending displacement, or geopolitical outcomes. The 2025 database replaces prior SIPRI military-spending data and should be treated as a new vintage.
